props.title: Rosetta
props.initialSlug: Intense portrait of a young woman's struggle for employment

sections.content: The Dardenne brothers' Rosetta (1999) revolutionized social realist cinema with its raw, unflinching portrayal of poverty and survival. Using handheld cameras that ruthlessly pursue Émilie Dequenne's desperate protagonist, the film established the Dardennes' signature style that would influence countless filmmakers. Like their later work Two Days, One Night (2014), it exposes the brutal economics of modern survival, but with an intensity that makes even their other films seem gentle in comparison. The film's impact was so immediate that it prompted Belgium to pass a "Rosetta Law" preventing employers from exploiting young workers.

sections.content: The influence of Rosetta extends beyond just subject matter into film language itself. Its aggressive, documentary-style camera movement created a new visual grammar for depicting social struggle, seen later in films like Fish Tank (2009) and The Wrestler (2008). The Dardennes strip away everything but the essential - no score, no establishing shots, just pure human desperation in motion. This approach revolutionized how filmmakers could approach stories of economic hardship. SUBHEAD: The New Social Realism Wave

Rosetta helped spark a new wave of unflinching social realist cinema across Europe. Films like 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days (2007) and The Death of Mr. Lazarescu (2005) from Romania's New Wave adopted similar techniques to expose systemic failures. In Britain, directors like Ken Loach with I, Daniel Blake (2016) and Andrea Arnold with Fish Tank (2009) carried forward this tradition of urgent, immediate storytelling about society's margins.
